# 2005A Question 14 {.unnumbered}

::: {.exam-question}
## Question {.question-label}

[**Describe**]{.task-verb} the compensatory mechanisms in a fit person moving from the supine to the standing position.
:::

:::: {#answer-structure}

## Suggested Structure

[**Describe**]{.task-verb} **Immediate Hydrostatic Effects**, **Circulatory Reflexes**, **Cerebral Compensation**, and **Muscle Pump and Venous Valves**. Present the time course and link each compensatory response to the disturbance caused by standing.

::::

## Examiner Comments

::: {.examiner-comments}
**52 %** of candidates passed this question.

This is slightly less than when the question was asked in 1998. As was highlighted in the previous examiners report, a complete answer required a level of synthesis and integration from several areas of physiology.

The main points that would gain a pass were:

- An appreciation that the circulation acts as a hydrostatic column of fluid subject to the effects of gravity
- Descriptions of the main circulatory effects of becoming upright
- Demonstration of an understanding of the circulatory compensation mechanisms involved
- Reference to the important cerebral compensations
- The contribution of the leg muscles and venous valves
- An idea of the time course and sequence of these events

Additional information that attracted further marks included:

- More detailed descriptions of the feedback mechanisms involved
- Numerical quantifications of the magnitude of the various pressure changes
- Identification of the conditions under which the physiological compensation mechanisms would be incomplete or disrupted
- An understanding of the relationship of the changes on intracranial pressure, cerebral perfusion pressure and venous pressure

Common mistakes or omissions included:

- Confusion over whether a decrease in blood pressure increases or decreases the rate of firing from the baroreceptors
- Pursuing one or two parameters in great detail, at the expense of a comprehensive overview
- Reproduction of graphs or formulae that, although relevant, are not accompanied by any description of the physiological implications of the interrelationship
- It should be noted that re-writing the question verbatim at the beginning of the answer does not attract marks
:::
